method: Option C hybrid — back-of-book Index (Burke 1945 pp. 540-551, extracted to /tmp/burke-index-only.txt) augmented by Phase 2 concept-extractions from 14 deep-unit JSONs and the unit-level concepts/positions arrays

tier_definitions.1: Load-bearing volume-wide — appears across multiple chapters; structural to dramatism's argument (the pentad, the ratios, substance, the four master tropes, etc.)
tier_definitions.2: Chapter-central — defines or dominates one chapter or one philosophical-school discussion

lemmas.etymology_or_greek_german_gloss: L. actus; Gk. energeia (actuality in operation); paired with Gk. dynamis (potency)
lemmas.gloss: First and most load-bearing pentadic term: the locus of motives; what is done. Burke distinguishes Act from sheer motion (Hobbesian/behaviorist reduction). An Act has form (Aristotelian morphe) and end (telos). The Act is the dramatic centerpiece: motives are not within agent or scene alone but within the Act.

Second pentadic term: the ground, setting, situation, or background within which the Act occurs. Synonyms include situation, terrain, environment, conditions. Scene-philosophy = materialism, in Burke's classification.

lemmas.etymology_or_greek_german_gloss: L. agens, from agere = to do/drive
lemmas.gloss: Third pentadic term: the actor, the doer, the person or kind of person performing the act. Agent-philosophy = idealism.
Fourth pentadic term: the means, instrument, or method by which the Act is accomplished. Agency-philosophy = pragmatism.

lemmas.etymology_or_greek_german_gloss: L. propositum; corresponds to Gk. telos (final cause)
lemmas.gloss: Fifth pentadic term: the end-in-view, the for-the-sake-of-which. Purpose-philosophy = mysticism (when raised to ultimate).  Burke distinguishes Platonist purpose (forms) from Neo-Platonist purpose (emanation-return).
Burke's five-term apparatus for analyzing motives. The five key terms of dramatism; the grammar through which any statement of motive can be analyzed for its pentadic featuring and ratios.

The proportional/causal/conditioning relation between any two pentadic terms; ten possible pairings (5C2). Burke uses ratios as principles of selectivity that govern how a motive-statement features one term as conditioned by another.
Burke's principal ratio: the act is implied by the scene that surrounds it; the scene is the container of which the act is the contained. Distinguished from act-agent ratio.
The agent is implied by the scene; the kind of agent fitted to the kind of scene. Source of Romantic-poetic pathetic-fallacy when scene-properties transfer to agent.
The act implies its agent; what a person does indexes what kind of person they are. Differentiated from scene-act ratio: the determinative-priority runs differently.
The act implies a means; the kind of act fitted to (or featured by) the kind of agency.
The act implies its purpose; the for-the-sake-of-which by which the act is featured.
The agent implies the means of action proper to that kind of agent.
The agent implies the purpose proper to that kind of agent.
The means implies the end; instrumentalist-pragmatist ratio par excellence.
The scene implies the means available; ground-conditions specify instrument.
The scene implies the purpose; situational-teleology.
Burke's name for the scene-agent ratio operating in lyric poetry where the speaker's inner state and external scene mirror each other.

lemmas.etymology_or_greek_german_gloss: L. sub-stantia = standing-under; Gk. hypostasis / ousia
lemmas.gloss: What a thing is; the standing-under-it that grounds its predicates. Burke shows that all substance-definitions paradoxically place the thing's definition outside itself (etymological 'sub-stantia' is what stands under it, not what it is). Center of Chapter 'Container and Thing Contained.'

The paradox that any substance-definition specifies the thing by reference to what it is not (sub-stans = standing under, but defined by what stands beside it as context, family, opposite). The motor of dramatistic dialectic.
Defining a thing by its surrounding context (its scene). Spinoza is paradigm: substance = that-by-which-defined-by-what-it-is-not.
Defining a thing by its family or stock (race, ancestry, biological lineage). The 'blood' definitions favored by Nazi ideology are critiqued as a familial-substance reduction.
Variant of substance whose ground is kinship/lineage.
Substance grounded in spatial-geometrical relations (Spinoza's Euclidean ethics); a positional-definitional variant.
Definition by location in a geometrical or proportional schema.
Substance defined by movement-toward or movement-from a direction; trends/tendencies as substance-terms. Movement is one variant.
Substance defined by its dialectical opposition to other substances; what a thing is by virtue of what it is not.
Variant of familial definition: definition by tribe/group/clan.
Definition by location in a system of relations.
Treating motives shared by all humans (death-fear, will-to-power, libido, etc.) as the substantial ground of action; analyzed and contested.
Burke's argument that substance, despite its paradoxes, is the indispensable center of motive-theory.
The persuasive-strategic dimension of substance-claims in political and theological discourse.
Title-image of the volume's opening chapter: the scene contains the act, the bottle contains the wine; container/contained as a scene-act schematic.
Burke's adaptation of Kant's antinomies to substance-definition: contradictions internal to any attempt to define an essence purely intrinsically.
Chapter title and methodological doublet: every motive-vocabulary involves a choice of scope (how wide an angle) and a corresponding reduction (what gets reduced out).

The choice of how wide a scene to set around the act; the size of the encircling background. Different circumferences (biological, sociological, theological, cosmological) yield different motive-vocabularies. Volume-spanning.

Translating a higher-order motive-vocabulary into a lower-order one (organic to atomistic, quality to quantity, mental to physical). One of the four master tropes (= synecdoche when treated as part-for-whole). Burke is suspicious of all reductive moves that misrepresent their domain.
Reducing organic wholes to atomic parts (the Hobbes-Lucretius-modern-mechanist strategy).
Reducing higher-order phenomena (mind, value, agency) to material processes; behaviorist or physicalist reductive move.
Reducing values to monetary measure; the cash-nexus reduction characteristic of capitalist motive-vocabulary. Burke's example of a circumference-shrinking reductive operation.
Reducing all motives to theological vocabulary; symmetric counterpart of materialist reduction.

The exemplary case around which a motive-vocabulary is built. Burke's criterion: a representative anecdote must be representative of the field it is meant to analyze (drama for human action, not lab-animal experiments). Volume-spanning methodological term.
An anecdote that serves as one's 'way in' to a subject; can be representative or unrepresentative.
Anecdote functioning as a terminus/endpoint of a motive-vocabulary's reach.

Burke's name for his method: treating language and thought as modes of action rather than means of conveying information. The Five Key Terms of Dramatism (the pentad) are introduced in the Introduction as the apparatus of dramatistic motive-analysis.

lemmas.etymology_or_greek_german_gloss: Gk. dialektike = the art of conversation
lemmas.gloss: Burke's general term for the to-and-fro of merger-and-division operations that constitute motive-analysis; equatable with dramatic. Co-extensive with one of the four master tropes (irony).
Title of Burke's chapter-length systematic treatment of dialectic; the place where Socratic transcendence, merger/division, and the four master tropes are systematically introduced.
Title of the constitutional chapter; the dialectic by which any constitution is positioned against opponents, predecessors, and idealized successors.
Burke's analysis of tragedy as a dialectical structure: action, passion, learning (poiema-pathema-mathema).
The dialectical operation by which an alien-other is constructed to bear away the community's tensions; division produced through ritual merger.
Marx-Engels-Lenin's official ontology; read by Burke as scene-stressed dialectic with an Agent-term (proletariat) supplying the upward turn.

Burke's most general dialectical operation: combining things (merger) and separating them (division). All dialectic reduces to these two moves and their interplay. The four master tropes are arranged around this axis.
Sub-types of merger: action-passion (Aeschylean), being-nothing (Hegelian), mind-body, etc.
Variant of merger where action and being-acted-upon are dialectically combined; structural to tragedy.
Hegelian variant of merger: being passes into nothing and vice versa as the opening dialectical pair.
Variant of merger: traditional Cartesian split treated as a merger-division axis.

Burke's appendix-elevated four master tropes: metaphor (perspective), metonymy (reduction), synecdoche (representation), irony (dialectic). Each functions both literally and as a meta-cognitive operation on motive-vocabularies.
First master trope. Literal sense: figurative speech. Meta-cognitive sense: perspective — seeing one thing in terms of another.
Second master trope. Literal: substitution of an associated term. Meta-cognitive: reduction — translating a complex order into an associated lower order.
Third master trope. Literal: part-for-whole or whole-for-part. Meta-cognitive: representation — a part stands in for the whole it represents.
Fourth master trope. Literal: saying the opposite of what one means. Meta-cognitive: dialectic — the perspective-of-perspectives by which terms imply their opposites.
Meta-cognitive equivalent of metaphor; viewing one thing from the angle of another.
Meta-cognitive equivalent of synecdoche; making-present-again by a stand-in part.

lemmas.etymology_or_greek_german_gloss: Gk. energeia = at-work-ness, activity in operation; dynamis = capacity/potency
lemmas.gloss: Aristotelian pair forming the act-potency axis. Burke makes this the most important Greek-philosophical donation to dramatism: every Act has actuality (energeia) and presupposes potency (dynamis) prior to its enactment.
Aristotelian-Thomistic doctrine: every act presupposes a prior potency that the act actualizes; the metaphysical structure of becoming.
Aristotle's term for the actuality of a thing carrying its proper end within itself; the fulfilled act. Foundational for the Act-Purpose ratio.
The end-toward-which an act moves; final cause; Aristotelian foundation of the Purpose-term in dramatism.
Aquinas's pair distinguishing act (dynamic) from status (resulting state). Burke deploys this as a structural-stable form contrast within Act-philosophy.

lemmas.etymology_or_greek_german_gloss: Gk. poiema = thing-made/act; pathema = thing-suffered; mathema = thing-learned
lemmas.gloss: Aeschylean tragedy-formula. Burke embeds this triad in dramatistic motive-analysis: agent acts, agent suffers, agent learns through suffering.
Scotus's individuating principle: the thisness of an individual that makes it just-this and not another instance of its kind.
The what-it-is of a thing; the essential nature; correlative to haecceitas (thisness).

lemmas.etymology_or_greek_german_gloss: L. essentia from esse = to be
lemmas.gloss: The what-makes-a-thing-what-it-is; classical philosophical term Burke discusses across philosophical schools (Santayana's essences, Thomist essence-existence distinction).
Counterpart to essence; the that-it-is over against what-it-is. Aquinas-Avicenna-Avicebron distinction.
Burke's term for translating essence-claims into temporal-developmental claims (essence-becomes-history). Hegelian and Marxian operation.
Philosophical school featuring Agent. Burke's classification: Plato through Berkeley through Kant through post-Kantian idealism (Fichte, Schelling, Hegel).
The philosophical-school move of treating the agent (mind, ego, subject) as the ideal-substantial ground of phenomena.
Hybrid school combining idealist and materialist features.
Philosophical school featuring Scene. Burke's lineage: Democritus, Lucretius (Epicurean materialism), Hobbes, Spinoza (transcended materialism), Darwin, modern behaviorism.
Epicureanism (atomistic-hedonist) and Stoicism (providential-materialist) as the two complete materialist systems of the Hellenistic age.
Philosophical school featuring Agency. Burke's lineage: Peirce, James, Dewey. The two principles of truth, instrumentalism, the cash-value-of-ideas formula.
Burke's survey of pragmatism's analytical scope.
Philosophical school featuring Purpose (when raised to ultimate-term status). Burke distinguishes mysticism of means (e.g., the perfect technique) from mysticism of ends (Neo-Platonist ascent).
Variant in which the means itself becomes invested with ultimacy (perfect technique, fetishized procedure).
The instant of unity-with-ultimate-term; James's Varieties is the principal datum.
School holding that universals are only names; particulars alone are real. Occam paradigmatic. Permanent dialectical pole opposed to realism.
School holding that universals have real being. Aristotle-Aquinas paradigmatic.
Burke's relabeling: the realist position is family-like (members share a common nature); the nominalist position is aggregate-like (members are merely collected).
20c version of realism keyed to scientific theory rather than scholastic universals.
School featuring reason as primary; verbal-medium-bound philosophy (Descartes-Leibniz-Spinoza-Kant).
Burke's analysis of the way rationalism is bound to the verbal medium of philosophical articulation.
Philosophical school resisting positive claims to knowledge; Hume's bundle-self and Santayana's animal-faith are paradigms.
British school grounding knowledge in sense-experience. Locke-Berkeley-Hume.
20c school combining logical analysis with empiricism (Vienna Circle, Neurath).
Modern psychology school reducing the human Act to stimulus-response; Burke's running negative example.
Bridgman's doctrine: meaning of a concept = operations used to apply it. Agency-philosophy in scientific dress.
Dewey's variety of pragmatism; ideas as instruments for action.
James-variant philosophical school centering personal-agent terms.
Scene-philosophy variant: motives grounded in natural processes alone. Darwin-Spinoza-Dewey lineage.
Counterpart of naturalism: extra-natural causal terms admitted.
Doctrine identifying God with the totality of nature/being; Spinozistic. Scene-philosophy in theological form.
Attribution of soul to natural objects.
Pre-Socratic doctrine: matter is living. Thales-tradition.
Aristotelian doctrine that every physical thing is form-in-matter. Implicit through Burke's Aristotle exposition.
The art form whose structural features (act, agent, scene, agency, purpose) furnish the master model for motive-analysis.
Dramatic form featuring suffering-and-learning; Burke's dialectic-of-tragedy analyzes its merger-and-division structure.
Burke's term for the pentadic-tension that sustains dramatic interest.
The dialectical end-point at which drama exhausts itself into pure dialectic.
Non-dramatic narrative form; Aristotle on the epic-drama distinction.
Poetic form in which scene-agent ratio dominates.
A founding instrument that constitutes a polity by its terms; Burke's chapter-length treatment makes constitutionality the chief mid-volume case-study for the dramatistic apparatus.
Variant constitutional schema rooted in syndicalist anarchism.
Unwritten common-law constitutional tradition.
Burke's chief test-case for the dialectic of constitutions; the document and its amendments treated as a representative anecdote.
Burke's name for the implicit constitutional principles operative behind the explicit constitutional text.

lemmas.lemma: Constitution addressed by agents to agents
lemmas.gloss: Burke's dialogic gloss on constitutional rhetoric.
Action outside the constitution that the constitution itself mandates.
A constitution that represents only some segment of the polity it claims to constitute.
The dialectic of one-and-many in constitutional polities.
Constitution-style featuring warnings and exhortations.
The legal-judicial conformity to constitutional terms.
The constitutional power to review legislation against the founding text. Marshall, John (Chief Justice) is the locus classicus.
Burke's analysis of federal-constitutional dialectic (Rougemont as interlocutor).
Modern political-economic system; treated as a constitutive motive-vocabulary.
Marxian political-economic system.
Theoretical program of Marx-Engels-Lenin; Burke supplies a dramatist grammar for Marxism in Ch. 5.
Modern political movement Burke treats as a perverse merger-formation.
Political-economic system; socialism-as-monetary-system is one of Burke's analytic moves.
Renaissance-and-modern intellectual tradition centering human agency.
Burke's chief modern god-term; money as substitute for God, as motive-substance, as ultimate-term within capitalist circumferences.
Motive vocabulary built around the money-term.
The cash-nexus ontology that money constructs.
Theological ultimate-term across multiple chapters; Spinoza's Deus-sive-Natura, Aristotle's God, Berkeley's divine perceiver, Aquinas's actus-purus all surveyed.
Legal-theological category for events outside human agency.
Theological tradition cross-referenced across the chapter on Aquinas and constitutions.
The ritually purged other; structural device by which a community projects its tensions outside itself.
Modern variant: the criminal as ritually-purged figure.
Ritual offering; in Burke linked to the collective-nature of war.
Faculty by which images are formed; Coleridge's primary and secondary imagination, Spinoza's imagination as the lowest of the three forms of knowledge.
Spinoza's tripartite forms of knowledge: imagination, reason, intuition.
Faculty of immediate intellectual apprehension; Spinoza's scientia intuitiva and Kant's Anschauung.
Discursive-inferential faculty; Spinoza's reason as the second form of knowledge; Hegel's cunning-of-reason.
Hegel's term: reason uses individual passions to achieve its historical ends.
Kant's category for the conditions of possible experience; transcends the empirical without being transcendent.
American philosophical movement (Emerson, Thoreau) centering Over-Soul; an idealism with Romantic-religious overtones.
Kant's move from theoretical to practical reason; the moral law as transcendent of phenomena.
Burke's name for the dialectical ascent through merger-and-division to an ultimate-term; the Platonic dialectical archetype.
Variant of the dialectical ascent specifically in Plato's dialogues.
The term at the summit of a dialectical hierarchy; what all subordinate terms ultimately mean by reference to.
Leibnizian windowless atom of substance; each monad mirrors the whole.
Leibniz's solution to monad-coordination: God pre-established harmony among the windowless monads.
Mind-body dualism Descartes inaugurated; res cogitans / res extensa.
Berkeley's idealist formula.
Hobbesian internal motion of body underlying appetite and aversion.
Hobbesian terms for the two directions of endeavor: toward/away.
Lucretian doctrine: atoms swerve unpredictably, allowing for freedom within an atomistic scene.
Ancient atomist ontology.
Santayana's term: the pre-philosophical trust the living organism extends to its surroundings.
Action mediated by symbols; central to Mead's social-psychology and to Burke's reading of the Keats Ode as 'Symbolic Action in a Poem.'
Mead's name for language: linguistic utterance as a species of physical gesture that mediates social interaction.
Korzybski's pedagogical apparatus (strings, plugs, tin) for diagramming meaning. Burke treats it as the type-case of a non-representative anecdote.
Korzybski's general-semantics program.
Korzybski's term for the neural substrate of semantic operations.
Korzybski's program of language-and-thought reform.
The Romantic-poetic device of attributing emotion to nature; Burke analyzes via the scene-agent ratio.
Korzybski's action-concept that Burke critiques as inadequate to dramatistic action.
Mead's term for outward-observable behavior.
Theological-cosmological act-type; James on the way of creation.
James's term for the mode of creative cosmological act.
The scenic/agent-conditions underwriting any creative act.
Agent's autonomous self-determination; classical theological-philosophical concept.
Volume-spanning political-philosophical category; Aristotle on freedom, Marx on freedom, Burke on capitalism-freedom and freedom-circumference.
Counterpart of freedom; Spinozistic necessitarianism.
Marxian doctrine of historical determination.
Modern-physics substitute for classical necessity; Heisenberg as data.
Necessity-claim with rhetorical weight.
Dialectical counterpart to inevitability; the unexpected within the necessitarian narrative.
Dramatic structure between inevitability and surprise.
Non-necessitarian causal element; ancient tuche.
Ancient providential-fate vocabulary.
Behaviorist motive-term Burke uses critically.
Pre-rational motive-term; treated alongside drives, urges, libido.
Freudian sexual-energy term.
Motive-term in the psychological-reductive lineage.
Freudian clinical category.
Freud's investigative-therapeutic discipline.
Freud's internalized authority-figure within the psyche.
Freudian self-as-organizer.
Jung's species-shared unconscious.
Freudian myth of an original murder-of-the-father grounding cultural prohibition.
Greek avenging-spirits; symbol of conscience.
Voluntarist motive-category.
Generalized agent-term; Meadian social-self plus mystical/Emersonian Self.
Spinozistic-Romantic motive-category.
Christian-tragic moral category.
Emerson's Transcendentalist ultimate-term.
Burke's name for the self-relating structure of mystic unity.
Burke's term for a triadic-imagistic figure in mystic-poetic discourse.
Burke's poetic figure for mystic pursuit.
Burke explores the role of negation in motive-vocabulary (Coleridge's, Spinoza's, Bergson's).
Bergsonian purposiveness embedded in the negative.
Chapter-portion on the variants of Purpose.
Purpose conceived as Platonic ascent to the Forms.
Purpose as emanation-and-return; the One issues forth and is returned to.
Aristotelian-Burkean term for the for-the-sake-of-which; treated dialectically with means.
Instruments; in dialectic with ends.
Pragmatist-instrumentalist program.
Burke's self-reflexive treatment of his own volume's ends and means.
Burke's analysis of symbolic dimension of agency-terms.
Burke's reading of mother-symbolism in agency-terms.
Erotic-symbolic dimension of motive-terms.
Greek term for being-together; used by Coleridge.
Coleridgean image of organic merger.
Knight's economic-tendency concept for partial acts.
The internal-to-X. Ch. 11 'Problem of the Intrinsic' treats the impossibility of pure intrinsic-only definition.
External-to-X; the unavoidable counterpart to any intrinsic claim.
Title of Burke's eleventh chapter; the impossibility of defining a literary work purely by its intrinsic features alone.
Chicago-school criticism (Crane, Olson, Maclean) that Burke addresses as primary interlocutor in Ch. 11.
Coleridge-Southey utopian project; Burke uses it as a constitutional-political case-study.
Pre-Marxian utopian socialists (Saint-Simon, Owen, Fourier).
Variants of forward-projecting motive-vocabulary.
Apocalyptic-eschatological forward projection.
Modern-progressive forward projection.
Burke's analytic name for a constitutive anti-war document.
Anti-war moral-political position.
Burke's analysis of war's representative-anecdote function in WWII-era constitutional thinking.
Constitutive anecdote linked to collective sacrifice.
Excessive deference to scientific method as universal vocabulary.
Hellenistic-imperial school featuring providential-materialism plus moral-agent doctrine.
Hellenistic school featuring atomistic-hedonist materialism.
Late-antique heterodox-Christian school featuring esoteric salvific knowledge.
Aquinas-derived theological-philosophical system.
Kant's mediating-image between category and intuition.
Reflexive perception of oneself perceiving; Kantian transcendental apperception.
Independent of experience; Kantian methodological category.
Berkeleian distinction between idea (image) and notion (concept).
Central British-empiricist term; in Berkeley = perception, in Hume = pale copy of impression.
Burke's name for the morphological family unifying substance / constitution / status / state / circumstance.
Stable condition resulting from an act; co-paired with actus in Aquinas.
Posture/standing; core member of the stance-family.
Hobbesian decaying-sense.
Affective motive-terms across Hobbes-Spinoza-Hume lineage.
Spinozistic taxonomy of the affects.
Negative affect; Spinozistic context.

lemmas.lemma: Active and passive terms in Spinoza
lemmas.gloss: Burke notes Spinoza's grammatical active/passive distinction as crucial.
Spinozistic principle: to determine is to negate.
Spinoza on how mind-knowledge transcends bodily affection.
Compound term for the mind-body merger problem.
Marshall's political-technical category.
Marxian collective-agent term.
Marxian: a class's self-recognition as agent.
Marxian dialectical conflict between classes.
Marxian central category.
Marxian social-formation.
Financial-system agency-instance.
Market-coordination mechanism.
Modern industrial-economic order.
Liberal-economic doctrine of minimal state intervention.
Capitalist market unconstrained by state.
Quasi-natural-law of market behavior.
Motive-vocabulary built around capital-accumulation.
Burke's diagnostic for pathologies of capitalist motive.
Legal-economic category.
Variety-among-elements; counter-pole to monetary-reductive homogeneity.
Maximum-circumference term.
Central Scene-term; Spinoza's Deus-sive-Natura, Aristotle's basic principles of nature, Coleridge's view of nature.
Personification of Nature as maternal agent.
Synonym for Scene; biological-ecological framing.
Synonym for Scene.
Methodological orientation focused on scene-conditions.
Synonym for Scene; geographical-political framing.
Practical-instrumental category.
Political agency of statecraft.
Inter-bloc geopolitical structure.
Legal category for non-human-caused events.
Synonym for Act (biological-evolutionary register).
Synonym for Act (psychological register).
Anti-theistic position.
Stateless political doctrine; Herbert Read.
Specific scapegoat-formation.
Nazi doctrine.
Familial-substance reduction critiqued.
Kantian phenomena.
Greek-tragedy structural pair.
Aristotle's four causes (material, formal, efficient, final) furnish the pentadic foundation.
Aristotelian: that-out-of-which.
Aristotelian: that-by-which (form).
Aristotelian: that-from-which (mover).
Aristotelian: that-for-which (end).
Scholastic definition-formula: define by stating genus and specifying difference.
Greek term for ordered speech, reason, account; foundational to Western philosophical vocabulary.
Aquinas's God as pure act with no admixture of potency.
Mosaic Ten Commandments.
Hebrew legal-religious code.
Christian foundational ethical-text.
Universalizable ethical principle.
Cardinal political-philosophical category; Plato's Justice in the Republic vs Sophists' Justice as advantage of the stronger.
Doctrine of the world as a whole.
Universalist political position.
Burke's mid-century framing of worldwide issues.
Hegelian conditional-qualifier.
Hegel's developmental world-Spirit.
Hegel's narrative of Spirit's self-realization across history.
Hegelian: act that participates in Spirit's universal development.
Methodological doctrine: wholes are prior to parts.
Ancient and modern atomic ontology.
Chemical-vocabulary motive-reduction (Hegelian usage).
Body-chemistry vocabulary.
Physical unit of work; motive-energy term.
Pragmatist methodology.
Modern-behavioral-pragmatist action-vocabulary.
Burke's example of a non-representative anecdote for human motives.
Experimentally-controlled scientific anecdotes.
Korzybski's general-semantics operation of extracting features.
Modern formal-philosophy school Burke positions dramatism against.
The symbolic dimension of action and motive; central register of dramatism.
Korzybski's vocabulary for general semantics.
Modern study of language.
Burke's understanding of language as vocal-gestural symbolic act.
Philosophy of art and the beautiful.
Verbal art-form central to Burke's literary chapters.
Sign-with-meaning; basic unit of symbolic action.
Pictorial-imaginative unit; central to mystic and poetic discourse.
Motive-vocabularies that idealize their object.
Theological-mystical vocabularies.
Compressed-rhetorical units summing up motive-positions (per Burke's discussion of role-summings-up).
Mirror-trope in tragic discourse.

Lombrosian psycho-physical criminality-theory.
Tragic-dramatic protagonist.
Political-symbolic agent-type.

Aristotelian developmental category.
Coleridge's neologism for the pantisocracy ideal (asses-and-betters, all equal).
Burke's geometric figure for dialectical pairing of circumferences.

The paradox in any absolutized term: it must invoke a relative for definition.
